lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月29日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 精 — 音読み: セイ、ショウ / 訓読み: （常用の訓読みなし） — refined, polished; essence. Sake begins with polishing the rice, 精米せいまい, and the whole grade system rests on how far the grain is milled.
  • 磨 — 音読み: マ / 訓読み: みが-く — to polish, to grind. Brewers say the rice is 磨みがかれた, "polished down," and the word even appears in product names, e.g. 獺祭だっさい 磨みがき二割三分にわりさんぶ.

ことば

  • 酒造好適米しゅぞうこうてきまい — rice suited to sake brewing; "sake rice." The formal term for varieties like 山田錦やまだにしき and 五百万石ごひゃくまんごく: large grains, low protein, and usually a clear starchy core. In everyday talk it's shortened to 酒米さかまい.
  • 精米歩合せいまいぶあい — polishing ratio. It's the percentage of the grain that remains, not what's removed: 60% means 40% was milled away. It's printed on labels and is one of the bases of the premium grades.
  • 心白しんぱく — the opaque white core at the center of a sake-rice grain. Its starch is loosely packed, so kōji mold can grow into it easily; a large, centered 心白 is prized.
  • 精米機せいまいき — rice-polishing machine. For sake this usually means a vertical mill, 縦型精米機たてがたせいまいき, which grinds slowly so the grains don't overheat or crack.

例文

心白しんぱくの大きな酒米さかまいを精米機でゆっくり磨き、精米歩合五十パーセントまで仕上げた。

We slowly polished sake rice with a large white core in the polishing machine, bringing it down to a 50% polishing ratio.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月30日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 糠 — 音読み: コウ / 訓読み: ぬか — rice bran. Everything the polishing machine grinds away becomes 糠. The brown outer layers are 赤糠あかぬか, used for animal feed and pickling; the paler inner layers are 白糠しろぬか, sold as rice flour for 煎餅せんべい and sweets. Its fats and proteins are exactly what brewers want gone from the grain.
  • 浸 — 音読み: シン / 訓読み: ひた-す、ひた-る — to soak, to steep. It's the kanji behind the soaking step before steaming, 浸漬しんせき.

ことば

  • 枯からし — the rest after polishing. Milling heats and dries the grain, so the rice is left for a few weeks to cool and take moisture back from the air. Skip it and the grains crack when they hit water.
  • 洗米せんまい — washing the polished rice to strip off the leftover 糠 powder. For 吟醸ぎんじょう rice it's done quickly in small batches, because the grain starts drinking water the moment it's wet.
  • 浸漬しんせき — soaking the washed rice before steaming. Breweries say しんせき; dictionaries also give しんし, and you'll hear both.
  • 限定吸水げんていきゅうすい — timed, limited soaking. Highly polished rice absorbs water fast, so it's soaked by stopwatch, sometimes for only seconds or minutes, and weighed to hit a target uptake (often around 30%). A hallmark of careful 吟醸 work.

例文

精米せいまいを終おえた米は二週間にしゅうかんほど枯からしてから洗米せんまいし、ストップウォッチを片手かたてに限定吸水げんていきゅうすいで浸漬しんせきする。

Once polished, the rice rests for about two weeks. Then it's washed and soaked with limited water absorption, stopwatch in hand.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月31日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 蒸 — 音読み: ジョウ / 訓読み: む-す、む-れる、む-らす — to steam. Sake rice is steamed, never boiled: steam softens the starch so kōji and enzymes can get to work, while each grain stays separate and fairly dry. Read ジョウ in 蒸気じょうき, steam, and in 蒸留じょうりゅう, distillation.
  • 甑 — 音読み: ソウ / 訓読み: こしき — the traditional rice steamer. A rare kanji you'll almost only meet in brewing and archaeology, but in a sake brewery it's everywhere.

ことば

  • 蒸米むしまい — steamed rice for brewing. Every grain that goes into sake passes through this stage, whether it becomes kōji, starter, or one of the mash additions. Note the 訓読み here: むしまい, not じょうまい.
  • 甑こしき — the big steaming tub, traditionally wooden, now often stainless steel. It sits on top of a 和釜わがま, an iron cauldron of boiling water, and steam rises up through the rice.
  • 外硬内軟がいこうないなん — "firm outside, soft inside": the ideal texture for 蒸米. The surface is dry and springy, so the grains don't stick together, but the core is fully cooked. Brewers check it by kneading a pinch into a flat cake, 捻ひねり餅もち.
  • 放冷ほうれい — cooling the steamed rice. It's spread on cloth or sent through a cooling machine, 放冷機ほうれいき, down to the temperature each use needs, warmer for kōji and cooler for the mash.

例文

甑こしきで蒸むし上あげた蒸米むしまいが外硬内軟がいこうないなんに仕上しあがっているか確たしかめてから、放冷ほうれいして麹室こうじむろへ運はこぶ。

After checking that the rice steamed in the koshiki has come out firm outside and soft inside, we cool it and carry it to the kōji room.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月1日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 掛 — 音読み: カイ (rarely used) / 訓読み: か-ける、か-かる — to hang, to put on, to add. In the brewery it marks the rice that is "added" straight into the starter and mash. Common sake word: 掛米かけまい.
  • 倒 — 音読み: トウ / 訓読み: たお-れる、たお-す — to fall over, to topple. Its sake moment is the end of the steaming season, when the steamer is symbolically "toppled": 甑倒こしきだおし.

ことば

  • 麹米こうじまい — rice that will be made into kōji, roughly a fifth to a quarter of all the rice in a batch. Brewers often give it their best, most highly polished rice, and some labels list it separately from the 掛米.
  • 掛米かけまい — steamed rice that goes straight into the starter and the mash instead of becoming kōji. It's the bulk of the rice in a batch.
  • 連続蒸米機れんぞくじょうまいき — continuous rice steamer: the rice rides a mesh belt through a tunnel of steam. Common at larger breweries. Note that 蒸 is read じょう here, unlike むし in 蒸米.
  • 甑倒こしきだおし — "toppling the koshiki": the last steaming of the brewing 季節きせつ. Once the steamer isn't needed any more, the hardest part of the season is over, and the 蔵くら usually celebrates with a small party.

例文

小さな蔵くらでは麹米こうじまいと掛米かけまいを毎朝まいあさ甑こしきで蒸むし、最後の蒸しが終おわる甑倒こしきだおしの日には、蔵人くらびとみんなで乾杯かんぱいする。

At a small brewery they steam the kōji rice and the mash rice in the koshiki every morning, and on the day of the last steaming, the whole brewing crew raises a toast together.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月2日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 麹 — 音読み: キク / 訓読み: こうじ — kōji: steamed rice grown through with mold. It's the heart of the craft; the old brewery saying is 一麹いちこうじ、二酛にもと、三造さんづくり: kōji first, the starter second, the mash third. You've already met it in 麹米こうじまい. Some labels and kōji products use the native-Japanese character 糀こうじ instead.
  • 室 — 音読み: シツ / 訓読み: むろ — room, chamber; as むろ, a warm, sealed room. In the 蔵くら it nearly always means the kōji room: 麹室こうじむろ.

ことば

  • 麹室こうじむろ — the kōji room: insulated, warm and humid, traditionally lined with 杉すぎ (cedar). Brewers usually just call it 室むろ.
  • 麹菌こうじきん — the kōji mold, Aspergillus oryzae. Its enzymes turn rice starch into sugar for the yeast to ferment. In 2006 the Brewing Society of Japan named it Japan's "national fungus", 国菌こっきん.
  • 種麹たねこうじ — kōji starter: dried spores of 麹菌こうじきん. Breweries buy it from specialist suppliers called 種麹屋たねこうじや, and only a handful of these remain in Japan.
  • 製麹せいぎく — kōji-making: the roughly two-day process in the 麹室こうじむろ. Note the reading: 麹 is ぎく here (its 音読み キク, voiced), not こうじ.

例文

蔵人くらびとは放冷ほうれいした蒸米むしまいを麹室こうじむろに運はこび、種麹たねこうじを振ふりかけて、二日かけて麹菌こうじきんを育てる。

The brewery workers carry the cooled steamed rice into the kōji room, sprinkle it with kōji starter, and spend two days growing the kōji mold.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月3日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 床 — 音読み: ショウ / 訓読み: とこ、ゆか — bed, floor. In the 麹室こうじむろ it's the long wooden work table, often cloth-covered, where the rice is spread, spored and kneaded. Brewers often call that table just 床とこ.
  • 揉 — 音読み: ジュウ / 訓読み: も-む — to rub, to knead (not a 常用 kanji, so it's often written in kana: もむ). In the 蔵くら it's the hand-kneading that works kōji spores into the rice, as in 床揉み（とこもみ）.

ことば

  • 引き込み（ひきこみ） — carrying the cooled steamed rice into the 麹室こうじむろ: the first step of 製麹せいぎく. Also written 引込み.
  • 種切り（たねきり） — sprinkling the 種麹たねこうじ over the rice spread on the 床とこ, usually from a fine sieve-like shaker so the spores fall evenly.
  • 床揉み（とこもみ） — rubbing the spores into the rice by hand right after 種切り（たねきり）, so every grain is coated. The rice is then heaped and wrapped in cloth to keep warm. Often written 床もみ.
  • 切り返し（きりかえし） — roughly half a day later the rice has warmed and clumped. The team unwraps it, breaks up the clumps to even out temperature and moisture, and wraps it again.

例文

引き込み（ひきこみ）を終おえた蒸米むしまいを床とこに広ひろげ、種切り（たねきり）と床揉み（とこもみ）をしたら、半日はんにちほどで切り返し（きりかえし）をする。

The steamed rice, now carried into the kōji room, is spread out on the bed; once the spores have been sprinkled on and rubbed in, the clumps are broken up and remixed about half a day later.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月4日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 盛 — 音読み: セイ、ジョウ / 訓読み: も-る、さか-る、さか-ん — to heap up, to serve into a dish; to flourish. In the 麹室こうじむろ it names the step where the growing kōji is portioned out into small trays: 盛り（もり）.
  • 蓋 — 音読み: ガイ / 訓読み: ふた — lid, cover. In sake it appears in 麹蓋こうじぶた, the shallow cedar tray the kōji grows in (the name likely comes from its lid-like shape).

ことば

  • 盛り（もり） — about a day after 引き込み（ひきこみ）, the kōji is divided into 麹蓋こうじぶた or larger boxes so heat and moisture can be controlled in small portions. Same idea as 盛る（もる）, "to dish out."
  • 麹蓋こうじぶた — a small, shallow tray of 杉すぎ (cedar), holding only a little rice. It's the most hands-on method (麹蓋法こうじぶたほう) and many breweries still use it for their top-grade kōji.
  • 仲仕事なかしごと — the "middle work," several hours after 盛り（もり）: the kōji is mixed and spread more thinly to release the heat the mold is now producing.
  • 仕舞仕事しまいしごと — the "final work," several hours after 仲仕事なかしごと: one last mix, spreading the kōji thin, often raked into ridges and furrows so it cools and dries evenly.

例文

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月5日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 破 — 音読み: ハ / 訓読み: やぶ-る、やぶ-れる — to break, tear. In the 麹室こうじむろ it describes mold "breaking into" the steamed rice: 破精はぜ, the white patches where 麹菌こうじきん has taken hold.
  • 突 — 音読み: トツ / 訓読み: つ-く — to thrust, pierce. It names 突つき破精はぜ, kōji whose mold pierces deep into the grain from just a few spots.

ことば

  • 出麹でこうじ — taking the finished kōji out of the room, roughly two days after 引き込み（ひきこみ）. The word also means the finished kōji itself.
  • 破精はぜ — the white, fuzzy areas where the mold has grown on and into a grain. Brewers look at both how much surface it covers and how deep it goes.
  • 破精込み（はぜこみ） — how deeply the mold has penetrated into the grain. Deep 破精込み means the enzymes reach into the rice's core, where they'll do their work in the mash.
  • 突つき破精はぜ — kōji with mold in scattered spots on the surface but reaching deep inside. Its moderate, steady enzyme power makes it the classic kōji for 吟醸ぎんじょう.
  • 総破精そうはぜ — kōji with mold covering the whole grain and penetrating deeply. Its strong enzymes give fuller, richer sake, and it is often used for 酒母しゅぼ.

吟醸ぎんじょう用ようの麹こうじは突つき破精はぜを、酒母しゅぼ用ようの麹こうじは総破精そうはぜを目指めざし、破精込み（はぜこみ）を確たしかめてから出麹でこうじする。

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月6日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 酛 — 音読み: なし / 訓読み: もと — yeast starter. A 国字こくじ, a character made in Japan, so it has no on-reading: 酉 (the wine jar) plus 元 (origin). It's the "二" in 一麹、二酛、三造り（いちこうじ、にもと、さんづくり）, and every starter method is named with it, starting with today's 速醸酛そくじょうもと.
  • 酵 — 音読み: コウ / 訓読み: なし — fermentation, leaven. Almost always paired with 母 in 酵母こうぼ, yeast, or with 発 in 発酵はっこう, fermentation.

ことば

  • 酒母しゅぼ — the yeast starter: a small, dense batch of kōji, steamed rice and water where a large, healthy yeast population is grown before the main mash. 酒母 is the formal term (you'll see it in brewery texts and on tours); 酛もと is the older brewers' word for the same thing.
  • 酵母こうぼ — yeast. The strain a kura chooses (often one of the numbered 協会酵母きょうかいこうぼ from the Brewing Society of Japan) shapes the aroma about as much as any other decision.
  • 乳酸にゅうさん — lactic acid. The starter has to be acidic so that wild yeasts and bacteria can't take over while the sake yeast multiplies. How that acid gets there is what separates the starter methods.
  • 速醸酛そくじょうもと — the "quick" starter method: ready-made lactic acid goes in at the very start, instead of waiting for lactic bacteria to make it. Developed around 1910, it takes about two weeks rather than about four, and most sake made today uses it.

例文

速醸酛そくじょうもとでは、まず仕込しこみ水みずに乳酸にゅうさんを加くわえて雑菌ざっきんを抑おさえ、その中で酵母こうぼを増ふやして酒母しゅぼを育てる。

In the quick starter method, lactic acid is first added to the brewing water to keep unwanted microbes in check, and the yeast is multiplied in that environment to raise the yeast starter.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月7日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 卸 — 音読み: シャ（常用外） / 訓読み: おろ-す — to unload, to grind down; also "to sell wholesale". In sake it's the 卸 of 山卸し（やまおろし）, the hard grinding work of the traditional starter. Outside the brewery you'll meet it in 卸売おろしうり, wholesale.
  • 廃 — 音読み: ハイ / 訓読み: すた-れる、すた-る — to abolish, to fall out of use. It's the 廃 in 山廃やまはい, short for 山卸廃止酛やまおろしはいしもと: "the starter where yamaoroshi was abolished".

ことば

  • 生酛きもと — the traditional Edo-period starter method. No acid is added: lactic acid bacteria from the brewery's own surroundings make the acid naturally, and only then does the yeast take over. It takes about four weeks and gives sake that is often richer and more savory. Note the unusual reading of 生 as き, as in 生一本きいっぽん.
  • 山卸し（やまおろし） — grinding the rice and kōji of a kimoto starter into a paste with wooden poles, done by brewers in shifts on cold nights. Also called 酛摺り（もとすり）.
  • 半切はんぎり — the wide, shallow wooden tubs where kimoto starters are made and ground; also written 半切はんぎり桶おけ. Shallow so the starter stays cold and is easy to work.
  • 山廃酛やまはいもと — the kimoto variant without yamaoroshi. Around 1909, researchers found that if the water and kōji are mixed first, the kōji's enzymes dissolve the rice on their own, so the grinding wasn't needed. On labels you'll usually see just 山廃やまはい.

例文

山卸し（やまおろし）の手間てまを省はぶいた山廃酛やまはいもとも、生酛きもとと同じく、蔵くらにいる自然しぜんの乳酸菌にゅうさんきんの力ちからで酒母しゅぼを育てる。

Yamahai, which skips the hard work of yamaoroshi, raises its yeast starter just like kimoto does, through the power of the natural lactic acid bacteria living in the brewery.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月8日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 樽 — 音読み: ソン / 訓読み: たる — cask, barrel. You'll know it from 樽酒たるざけ, sake aged briefly in cedar casks, but inside the kura it also names barrel-shaped tools, like today's 暖気樽だきだる.
  • 湧 — 音読み: ユウ / 訓読み: わ-く — to well up, to gush (as a spring does). Brewers use it for a starter that comes alive with bubbling fermentation: 湧き付き（わきつき）.

ことば

  • 打瀬うたせ — the cold holding period of a traditional 生酛 or 山廃 starter. For a week or two the starter rests at a low temperature while natural lactic acid bacteria make acid and keep unwanted microbes out, before any warming begins.
  • 暖気樽だきだる — a small barrel filled with hot water and set into the starter to warm it gently, step by step, on a daily schedule. Note the special reading of 暖気 as だき. Today it's often stainless steel rather than wood.
  • 湧き付き（わきつき） — the point when the yeast takes over and the starter starts fermenting in earnest: bubbles, rising temperature, a fresh fermenting aroma. The verb form is 湧き付く（わきつく）.
  • 分け（わけ） — near the end, dividing the starter into smaller vessels to cool it quickly and calm the fermentation, so the yeast stays healthy until the starter goes into the main mash.

例文

打瀬うたせが終わった酛もとを暖気樽だきだるで少しずつ温あたためていくと、やがて湧き付き（わきつき）を迎え、最後に分け（わけ）で冷ひやされる。

Once its cold resting period is over, the starter is warmed little by little with a hot-water barrel until it finally springs into active fermentation, and at the end it is split into smaller vessels to cool down.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月9日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 醪 — 音読み: ロウ / 訓読み: もろみ — fermenting mash. Once the starter is finished, rice, kōji and water are added to it in the tank, and this main fermentation is the 醪もろみ. Today we leave the 酛もと behind and step into the tank. (It's often written in kana, もろみ, or as 諸味もろみ.)
  • 添 — 音読み: テン / 訓読み: そ-える、そ-う — to add, to go along with. In the kura it names each addition of rice, kōji and water to the mash. Notice that it becomes ぞえ in compounds: 初添はつぞえ.

ことば

  • 三段仕込み（さんだんじこみ） — three-stage mashing: rice, kōji and water go into the tank in three batches over four days, each one bigger than the last. Adding everything at once would dilute the yeast and the protective acidity; going step by step keeps the mash healthy. It's the standard method in almost every kura.
  • 初添はつぞえ — the first addition, on day one. The starter goes into the tank with the first, smallest batch, kept fairly warm (around 12°C) so the yeast gets going. Often shortened to 添そえ.
  • 踊り（おどり） — "the dance": day two, a rest day. Nothing is added, and the yeast multiplies. Brewers check the mash's condition before continuing.
  • 仲添なかぞえ — the second, middle addition on day three, about twice the size of the first and cooler (around 9–10°C). Also just 仲なか.
  • 留添とめぞえ — the third and final addition on day four: the largest batch, at the coldest temperature (around 7–8°C). Also just 留とめ. From here the 醪 ferments on its own for several weeks.

例文

初添はつぞえの翌日よくじつは踊り（おどり）といって仕込み（しこみ）を休み、酵母こうぼが増えるのを待まってから仲添なかぞえ、留添とめぞえと進めていく。

The day after the first addition is the "dance": the brewers take a break from adding to the mash and wait for the yeast to multiply, then move on to the middle addition and finally the last one.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月10日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 泡 — 音読み: ホウ / 訓読み: あわ — foam, bubble. After the 留添とめぞえ, the 醪もろみ foams up in recognizable stages, and brewers read the foam as a gauge of how fermentation is going (高泡たかあわ, 泡あわなし酵母こうぼ).
  • 複 — 音読み: フク / 訓読み: （常用の訓読みなし） — multiple, compound, double (as in 複雑ふくざつ, complicated). In sake it's the 複 of 並行複発酵へいこうふくはっこう, the double fermentation that makes sake special.

ことば

  • 並行複発酵へいこうふくはっこう — multiple parallel fermentation. Kōji enzymes turn starch into sugar (糖化とうか, saccharification) while yeast turns that sugar into alcohol, both at the same time in the same tank. Beer does the two steps one after the other (単行複発酵たんこうふくはっこう). Doing them together is why sake can reach around 20% alcohol.
  • 高泡たかあわ — "tall foam": the stage a few days to about a week into the mash, when thick, sticky foam piles up high above the surface at the peak of fermentation. Its height and texture tell the brewer how vigorous the yeast is.
  • 泡消あわけし機き — foam breaker: a rotating device fitted at the rim of the tank that knocks the foam down so it doesn't spill over.
  • 泡あわなし酵母こうぼ — low-foam yeast: strains selected so they don't form tall foam (for example 協会きょうかい701号, the foamless version of No. 7). The tank can be filled fuller, and the brewer saves the work of watching and cleaning foam.

並行複発酵へいこうふくはっこうが盛さかんになると醪もろみは高泡たかあわを迎え、泡あわが溢あふれないように蔵人くらびとは泡消あわけし機きを取とり付つける。

🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月10日  
  漢字  
  泡 — 音読み: ホウ / 訓読み: あわ — foam, bubble. After the 留添（とめぞえ）, the 醪（もろみ） foams up in recognizable stages, and brewers read the foam as a gauge of how fermentation is going (高泡（たかあわ）, 泡なし酵母（あわなしこうぼ）).
  複 — 音読み: フク / 訓読み: （常用の訓読みなし） — multiple, compound, double (as in 複雑（ふくざつ）, complicated). In sake it's the 複 of 並行複発酵（へいこうふくはっこう）, the double fermentation that makes sake special.

  ことば  
  並行複発酵（へいこうふくはっこう） — multiple parallel fermentation. Kōji enzymes turn starch into sugar (糖化（とうか）, saccharification) while yeast turns that sugar into alcohol, both at the same time in the same tank. Beer does the two steps one after the other (単行複発酵（たんこうふくはっこう）). Doing them together is why sake can reach around 20% alcohol.

  例文  
並行複発酵（へいこうふくはっこう）が盛（さか）んになると醪（もろみ）は高泡（たかあわ）を迎え、泡（あわ）が溢（あふ）れないように蔵人（くらびと）は泡消し機（あわけしき）を取（と）り付（つ）ける。

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月11日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 櫂 — 音読み: トウ / 訓読み: かい — oar, paddle; in a brewery, the long wooden paddle used to stir starters and mash. Not a 常用 kanji, and the on-reading is almost never used: in sake it's always かい. Common sake word: 櫂入れ（かいいれ）.

ことば

  • 櫂入れ（かいいれ） — stirring the mash with a paddle. Done through 三段仕込み（さんだんじこみ） and the moromi period to even out the temperature and mix rice, kōji and yeast; ginjō brewers keep it gentle and infrequent.
  • 櫂棒かいぼう — the paddle itself: a long pole with a flat board at the end. Many breweries now also mix by machine or with air, but the 櫂棒 is still the classic tool.
  • 品温ひんおん — the temperature of the mash itself (not of the room). Brewers record it every day; a ginjō moromi is kept cold, around 10°C or a little above at its peak.
  • 日本酒度にほんしゅど — sake meter value, a specific-gravity reading taken with a hydrometer, the 日本酒度計にほんしゅどけい. It starts far into the minus side and climbs as the sugar ferments away. On a finished label, plus leans 辛口からくち and minus leans 甘口あまくち, though acidity changes how it actually tastes.
  • 醪日数もろみにっすう — the number of days of moromi fermentation, usually counted from 留添とめぞえ to pressing. Roughly three weeks for everyday sake; a month or more for cold ginjō mashes.

例文

醪日数が進むにつれて、蔵人くらびとは毎日品温と日本酒度を測はかり、櫂入れの回数かいすうを調整ちょうせいする。

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月12日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 槽 — 音読み: ソウ / 訓読み: ふね (brewers' reading; not a 常用 kun-reading) — tank, vat, trough. The moromi is finished, so today we start pressing: 槽 appears in the formal word for pressing, 上槽じょうそう, and on its own, read ふね, it is the brewers' press box. Outside sake you know it from 水槽すいそう, a fish tank.
  • 搾 — 音読み: サク / 訓読み: しぼ-る — to squeeze, to press. 搾しぼる is the everyday verb for pressing sake, and 搾りたて（しぼりたて）, "freshly pressed," is a common label word in winter.

ことば

  • 上槽じょうそう — pressing: separating the finished moromi into clear sake and lees. This is the formal brewing term; brewers also just say 搾り（しぼり）.
  • 槽搾り（ふねしぼり） — pressing in a 槽ふね, a long box, traditionally wooden, now often steel. Bags of moromi are stacked inside and pressed slowly from above. Gentle but laborious; many breweries now use an accordion-style automatic press instead, 自動圧搾機じどうあっさくき.
  • 酒袋さかぶくろ — the cloth bag filled with moromi for pressing in a 槽 or for hanging. Traditionally cotton, now usually synthetic fabric.
  • 袋吊り（ふくろづり） — hanging the filled bags and letting the sake drip out by its own weight, with no pressure at all. Used for competition sake and top 大吟醸だいぎんじょう; the drops collected this way are sold as 雫酒しずくざけ.

例文

この蔵くらでは今も槽搾りで上槽し、特別な大吟醸だいぎんじょうだけは袋吊りで搾しぼる。

At this brewery they still press in a traditional press box, and only the special daiginjō is left to drip from hanging bags.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 11月13日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 粕 — 音読み: ハク / 訓読み: かす — lees, dregs (not a 常用 kanji). Whatever stays behind in the bag after pressing is 粕: the word is 酒粕さけかす, sake lees. On its own the on-reading ハク is almost never used; read it かす.
  • 責 — 音読み: セキ / 訓読み: せ-める — to press hard, to torment; responsibility. You may know it from 責任せきにん. In the press it names the last, hardest-squeezed portion of sake: 責め（せめ）.

ことば

  • 荒走り（あらばしり） — the first sake to run from the press, before any real pressure is applied. Usually a little cloudy, lively and fresh, sometimes slightly fizzy. Often bottled separately and sold under this name in winter.
  • 中取り（なかどり） — the middle run: clear, balanced, considered the best part. Breweries often choose it for competition sake. Also called 中汲み（なかぐみ）.
  • 責め（せめ） — the last run, pressed out under the strongest pressure. Heavier and with more rough edges (雑味ざつみ), it is usually blended rather than bottled alone.
  • 酒粕さけかす — sake lees: the white cake of rice, kōji and yeast left after pressing. Pressed into sheets it is 板粕いたかす; in the kitchen it becomes 粕汁かすじる, lees soup, and a kind of 甘酒あまざけ.

例文

槽搾り（ふねしぼり）では荒走り、中取り、責めの順じゅんに酒が出てきて、酒袋さかぶくろの中には酒粕が残る。

In box pressing, the sake comes out as the first run, then the middle run, then the hard-pressed last run, and the sake lees stay behind in the pressing bags.
